02:20 - Planned vs. unplanned breaks
03:45 - Building systems & relinquishing control
05:45 - Batching evergreen content & guest hosts
08:35 - Seasonality & managing workloads
10:15 - Audience engagement & viewer expectations
12:15 - Preparing to return to your space
14:00 - Protecting your well-being & boundaries
15:35 - Communicating with your viewers
17:05 - Break-proofing content & back catalogs
19:35 - Treating your comeback like a premiere
21:25 - Rebuilding sustainable habits
transcript: I want to talk to you about something that comes up a lot with creators,and that is the idea of taking a break.And I know we can't be prescriptive about this because every creator is different,every channel is different, every audience is different.But there will come a time in almost every creator's career where either they wantto make sure they take regular breaks,they are forced to take a break by life and other circumstances,or they just end up in a point where a break is necessary for themto figure out what comes next.So how do you look at breaks for creators?Yeah, I mean, I would say this is one of the biggest questionsthat we tend to get. I think it's one of the hardest ones to answerbecause it's another one of those where there isn't so much, hey, do A, B,and C, it is very much okay.Step one. Let's sit downand contextualize situation. What what is it that is motivating you to take a break?You covered some of them.Like it could be life events.It could be that you really are just burnt out physicallyor mentally from the toll creating content.It could be that, as you said, you need time to actually likerethink what your strategy is. So I think step one,interrogate and be honest yourself.What is that thing? A lot of creators I've talked to will say I need to take a break,but it's rare that they know why.It's kind of like step one. I know I need to do something,something needs to change. And so it's really asking the why.And then the next step is asking yourself like, what is the what?So is this a reduction?Like we have a resource where we talk about kind of the ways to go about this.And you can talk about a reduction in your uploads.So it's like, hey, I want to, I want to keep my foot on the gas, but I want to like,ease up a little bit, take some pressure off myselfand shift to more lightweight content model.Or is this a situation where you really have to have an extended break,whether that looks like a couple of weeks, whether it looks like longer.And so once you know what that is and kind of what feels realisticand attainable for you,then you can start to kind of go down.All right, what are the considerations in each path? But I tend to start there.And I think one thing is like honesty with yourself.So a number of creators I've talked to are like,I need to take a break.They go, they make the video, they go away for two weeks and then they're back at itand it's like, is that really effective?Like what? What is a real break for you?What's going to be effective to overcome whatever situation youfind yourself in and what can you sustain?Because there are also like,I'm guilty of this as well, like people whoon vacation actually start thinking about work or kind of disconnect.And so that is something also to think about, like,don't sign up for a six month break if you're going to be back on.Yeah.I think that's really valid. I think there's like two sorts of breaksjust to speak broadly, like the expected breaks where there's a life event change.Like for example, I got this joband I just did not have time to do as much on my channel.And I had to account for that.And we can talk about that more later. But I was, I took like a threemonth break, then a six month break, then a nine month break.But maybe you got married.Maybe you had a kid, maybe you had a change of circumstance, allthese different reasons and then unplanned breaks,like something unexpected happened.And you're, you're going out and you have to learn to handle it.And one of the things I found early is I had to figure out what kind of person I was,because there I think, again, broadly speaking, there's two types of creators.One who like. in order to relax, they have to know that it's handled.And that means either like putting scheduled posts up justto like update their like putting out that video to say I'm takinga break, putting up posts or bulk recording videosso that maybe people don't even notice they're on break, butlike, they just know things are happening and otherswho want to like the whole concept of a break is I am not doing anything.I am not bulk loading, I'm not scheduling, I'm not checking in, throwing.The laptop. In the ocean.And if I think about that,that is not so like one is stressed by not having it managedand the other is stressed by managing it and finding outwhich one of those types you are is super helpful.You bring up a good point too, because barring the scenario,which is a tough one where it's just unexpected out of left field,something has happened.A big part of taking a break,or when I talk to creators about it, is actually trying to.It's not about the moment of taking the break.It's about putting the systems in place that either enable you to not haveto take the break or empower you to feel confident in that scenario.The first scenario you're talking about to take the break.And so that looks like having systems in place where, okay,if you're a single creator,like being okay with eventually getting to a place where you're handing off editingor handing off some of the writing and,and moving into a place where not everything has to fall on your shoulders.And just that alone, whether that's building a team around yourself,whether that's around going to fewer uploadsor being okay with uploading on a less frequent schedule,those all immediately remove stress off of you.And they're like, kind of easier ways to almost like microdose the break.And I microdose like the loss of control.And then when you see like, okay, that's like nothing caught on fire, it worked out.You kind of train yourself to be like, okay,I'm okay with relinquishing a little bit more control,a little bit more control, a little more control.And then when you do come into a scenario where it's like, I have to immediatelytake a break, you know, my team has it.I have systems in place like nothing's going to go wrong, everything will be there.So it's a little bit of like the training leading up to the breakor before the break to prevent it.And then there's also the like.Yeah, relinquishing control and being prepared for like those moments.There's some for the planned breaks.There are some like really big creators who are very public about like,I'm going to go on mat leave.I work for myself. So mat leave for me is instead of recording one podcast a week,I've been recording two podcasts a week for the last three months,and they're going to come out as I'm going on mat leave.So you're going to still see new things.Or another one famously would get guest hosts like creators that they loved,and they would have that creator make a video for their channel,and those videos would go up while they were having a break.For others, it's like changing the banner to say,I'm taking a break or posting a video like the last video is I'm taking a break,or the last comment is I'm taking a break.So like what you said, some sort of process around controllingexpectations during that break?Yeah, I think all those examples you talked about are all kindof those elements you can kind of distill into different categories, right?So there is like having a planand you always want to have the plan before the scenario arises, right?And then there is essentially like understanding within your content.So like this is part of planning, but like, can your contentactually support the addition of a new face or a new voice?Or can someone cover for you in those instances, or can you bulk shoot the content?I think there are certain people, if you're making,you know, for example, like history essaysor longer form content that isn't necessarily focused on the topicalityof the moment. Yes, it's much easier.I use the term easy. It is conceivable that you could shoot some of that contentand release it on a schedule, right?Whereas if you do something that is current events and immediateless likely a strategy.So you need to think about like, okay, cool. How important is it that I have like mein the video? And can I bring someone inor another voice or use this to test other types of content that enable meto still do the topicality while I take a step away or move away?Yeah, for me, I was doing very newsy content,which is easy because I never had to think like what video to make.It was always just what was in the news. But when I decided to do the bulk recording,it was very evergreen, like buyer's guide sort of content.And at first it did like miserably because it wasn't what my audience expected.But looking back a year later, they all became like my highest performing.Because they just.Kept buying, because they just kept.Yeah, people just kept watching it.So I think like, even if it's not obvious, if you do have that ability,because obviously I'm not I can't pre-record news.I think I can make it up.That's a whole different channel.But but being willing to take that risk really did pay off.Did you ever consider I'm curious, when you were going into that,did you ever consider bringing another voice onto the channel?Because like so much of what your channel is,is trust in you that you are giving like the correct factual information.Did you consider another voice or was it always like,I think I need to go this evergreen route?I did like, so a different break that I took.I prerecorded a bunch of podcasts where it was like they weren't really podcastsbecause they were like, just me with another person discussing something.But that did give me like a,they were easier to produce than traditional buyers guides,but they did give me enough content to last like two monthswhile I was out doing something else.And it was just me with a different other creator every week.Got it. Okay. Yeah. Was that I'm curious, like from a mental standpoint,was that hard for you or did it feel like that was this was the right decision?It's, it was different.Like it ultimately was the right decision.I thought that it would be easier because I wouldn't have to carrythe videos alone. But it turns out scheduling other people is its owndifferent kind of work.Yeah.And that's an interesting point.Like how do you. This is something I've talked to creators about.I'm curious how you contend with this. I'll talk a little abouthow I think about it, but there is also this element of.So I used to have a crew of like 12 editorswho used to work for me at my previous job, and we hadto release videos constantly all through December.And naturally, like Holiday break is coming up,these editors are all working overtime to take the break.Like they needed to work overtime on the content, to be able to have content to post,to take the break. So how do you think about balance, like load balancing that,that like you're almost adding more stress on yourselfto be able to take the time off?How did you contend with that? And I'll talk a little about how I think about like.Yeah, it's interesting because like another, like one stepbefore take a break is also sometimes rebalance.Like I want a different sort of work life balance and other.We've also talked about just generally speaking with, with justlike how YouTube works is there is an element of seasonality, like in my industry,it was like right after the holidays, no one wanted to likecare about tech anymore.So like you always got the worst ad rates and the worst viewership rightafter the holiday, like right after the big holiday, like shopping period.So I would plan my breaks for then.And I've heard other creators say the views are terrible.So I'm going to I'm going to take my break like first month.And I would. So at first I just took a break then.But then I started doing like the bulk uploadingand the buyer's guides and things. Then because it let me plantthose evergreen videos when there was much less news and much less focus on my area.Got it. So you're using kind of the downtime to essentially.Work as normal, but it paid off exponentially because it was evergreen.And it's also interesting because in that moment, you're alsorealizing that the the stakes are low in the sense of like,I'm not necessarily this isn't the highest ad rate time for me.So if a video doesn't perform or if I don't post something,it's not necessarily going to like negative impact me from a revenue standpoint.Yes, absolutely. Like why waste the big shows for the, for like the worst time slots?And I think as with everything, like whether whatever topic we're discussing, right?It's always kind of about like bringing yourself into it bit by bit.And so that was kind of what I was going to talk about is in that planning,knowing and testing the various facets of your business before you take the break.That's a great example of like, okay, I know that ad rates are low.I know this is a slower time.This is a slower time for viewership or for the industry broadly.And I'm just going to not post a video this week.And stakes are low and let's see what happens.And you'll see that in 99.9% of cases, nothing catches on fire.Nothing goes wrong. Everything was all good. And that will giveyou trust. Like, okay, I ripped the Band-Aid off and when I needto take breaks down the line, I can know that like,I'm not going to be punished algorithmically.My audience is still going to come back and be here for me. And as longas I can communicate. And we talked a little bit about this, butcommunication is a major part of any break.As long as I communicate to my audience and they're not guessingwhere I'm at or seem confused, then ultimately,like I can breathe easyand take the space that I need to focuson the other parts of my life or focus on myself.And I think like the system is not designed to say like, oh,it's been a certain amount of time since your last upload, right?Therefore, we're going to decelerate you on your next upload again,because like there are creators who upload three times a yearand get like tens of millions of views.Like the system really does want to put a video that it believes that you're goingto be interested in, satisfied by, and want to watch more of that kind of stuff.That's like everyone's interests are aligned here.Yeah. It's not like there's tax brackets where it's like,I've taken 29 days off and if I take the 30th,it bumps me into another algorithmic thing.Like that's not how it works.No, not at all. Yeah. It's very video and topic centric,not very creative or channel centric.It is the number one concern of anyone taking a break. I thinkit's why we see some creators push themselves to continue posting.And you know, there is this element of for YouTube,we have every incentive that when you take a break and come back,we want viewers to know that their favorite creator is back,that this content is here. Connect them with the content they love.However, at the same time, your audience is your does have changing interests,changing passion. Like in that time that you're down, there are othercreators in your space who maybe posting content that they mayconnect with, they may engage with.And so I think that there is a real honest, there's a real,be honest with yourself that you're not going to immediately come back to immediate,massive viewership. Now, it's possible that if you have the right kind of content,the right kind of audience, and that's what we were talking about,like that deeper audience connection of people who are waiting for you to be there.But I think that you should expect some dip in viewershipand give yourself space to understand that that's going to be what may happenand talk through. Okay, that's going to happen.I need to like reengage with my audience.I need to start posting content. And that viewership will comeback if the content fits in the space.Now it depends. Like how long is the break lasting for?Has the space evolved? Has have things changed?And I think that's also why when we talked about coming back,you don't necessarily want to just throw yourselfback into creating content.You as you tail off your break, want to set time for like, okay, cool.I'm coming back into this space and let's say I'm a gamer.Let's say I do beauty content. I do history memes.Like what has that, what has happened in the time that I've been gone?Has the space evolved? Is there a new face? Is there someonewho's like been dominant?Is there a type of content that is really resonating with people?Is something happened in the broader, like political geo situation that like,I need to be aware of all of those things can inform you.And then there may be an evolution that comes with that,and there may be some time for you to catch up.But I think that ultimately, as, as we said earlier,this is not the system wanting to punish you like you stop uploading.So we're going to throttle your views.It is, hey, you need to reconnect with that viewership.You need to shake the rust off and kind of be ready to jump back into itand get going.Yeah, I think that rust.I think there are some creators who like the minute they sensea camera, they're in go mode and like they could take a year offand then hit the mic hot every time.There are other creators who like warm in warm out.So like, if you need to like record a video you never put up,that's one way to get back in the saddle if you need to build a habit back again,if you're not used to it,if you need to watch a bunch of YouTube to see what's going on now, what's hot now,if you need to go through the audience tab and look at like,what are my viewers watching?Which of my current videos are drawing in the most new users?Which other channels are they watching?Go to trends and see what what's hitting with people?Like give yourself that foundation and then try,like try that banger to see if you can ignite things immediately.If they don't like, go into build mode and video after video, just build,rebuild that connection.Yeah. And I think, look, it is about there's this kind of two pools, right?Because on the one hand, we're saying you could take away from this like, hey,the longer I stay away, the more chance there is for someone elseto come into the space and my audience lose interest at the same time.The original intention isto take, you're taking a break for a reason, so never lose sightof that reason that you are taking the break. And be honestwith yourself that like if you were to come back earlyor if you were to shorten your break, is it actually going to achieve the goal?Because your goal is to make content, your goal is also to takecare of yourself. And so sure, you can cut your break from,let's say a month down to one week and maybe get a little bit of disconnect in thereand you jump straight back into it and you feel kind of like,yeah, I didn't get rusty.I'm back in it. But how long is that sustainable?If you were feeling burnt out going into that,are you going to need to take another break a month from nowand then a month from now?So like, give yourself the maximum amount of time that you feel you need not onlyto take care of yourself, but also to do the things that you've been talking about.I've been talking about, like to do the research, to understand, to plan,to think of what is a good work life balance.What's the new production process for me?What's the research that needs to be done to kind of come upwith some new concepts or build a team?I think don't be afraid of longer breaksbecause it's really just about like solving that problem that caused you to goon the break in the first place. And that should be the priorityabove all else, not how many views can I get when I come back?Yeah. I think also realize that you can share anything you want to,but you do not have to share anything you don't want to.So you can bring your community, your audience along with you on the break.But having boundaries isn't a bad thing.Like you don't have like you get to choose.No one has a right to your information.But if you have a story you want to share while you're out or when you come back,like why I was out, what happened?Those sorts of things. Think about that as a potential decision.Maybe you don't want to talk about it at all.Maybe you want to have like a whole video dedicated to it.Those are all choices that we get to make as creators.That goes back to the communication point, and I think communication is key.But to your point, communication does not mean you need to do an houron the situation that you're in or why you're taking the break.I've seen really, really good.Taking a break videos that are 30s longand they're just appended to an existing video.And I've seen really amazing,in-depth kind of discussions that creators hadwith their audience about why they're taking the break. And itcomes down to, as you said, what you're comfortable sharing, what is goingto resonate in the moment.And I think it also comes down to the scenario you find yourself in.Yeah, yeah. There are people who will notice that you're gone.And there are people who will not notice that you're gone.There are just a lot of people who don't watch every video or like,they just don't pay that much attention.Your core fans are the ones who care the most,and they will pay attentionand they will let other people know. So I think it's always worthsort of thinking about them.And my other thing that I love to do is I don't like reinventing wheels.So a lot of times I will just look at like YouTube is the mosteasily accessible entertainment and information platform ever,but it's by no means the first one.And a lot of these lessons were learned for peoplewho were entertainers well before YouTube.Like the reason there are TV show seasons is because of seasonality.And the reason, like late night talk shows could have guests was like,these are like not totally solved problems, but these are understood problem spaces.And so a lot of this was like, when is the seasonality for me?When can I have guests?Like, how is this handled?Like, how do people react to these things?And I think that brings us to the other part of like, how do you come back?I think before we talk about how we come back,one thing that you touched on that I think is really interesting is alsoalmost break proofing your content in the sense of, if we go to you as the example,people trust your perspectiveand your opinion on the content you're creating.So they're coming for you.And what you have to say about like,everybody will be talking about a topic or maybe engaging in something,but like they want to hear Renee's perspective on it.And that's another thing to think about as a creator.When you look at your content, when you're doing a broad content strategy overview,what is the audience coming for?What is it about me that they're connecting with? And if you're questioninglike, are they might just be here for the IP, they may just be here for the trend.And I'm always chasing like that thing.Then start to think about how you can inject more of yourself in person into it.It feels almost counterintuitive, but the more you inject into yourself,the more then the audience is goingto be willing to be like, okay, cool.Like this person is gone,but I want to wait for them to come back and see their content again.So like, the more you put into it, the more you can step away down the line,which feels counterintuitive, but like, yeah, that will then help you stand out.Otherwise, if it's one of 15 trend channels that I watch,I'll just go to the next trend channeland kind of roll through it. So I think that's also a big elementof like making sure that you are providing unique value as the creatorand that you're injecting your point of view and perspectiveuniquely into the conversation.And that's if you're not doing that today,or you look at your content and you're worried about that, you can solve that.Like you have an audience, you have the ability, you have the hard part done.Now start kind of injecting that in and you'll start to build that deeper community.Who will be there to support you when you take a break?You want to as much like it's very difficult, but you want to,as much as possible, be a destination.And also like I was doing very like short shelf life news focused content,but I did the long shelf life, evergreen content as well,because if you can build up a substantial back catalog of evergreen content,the base layer of your revenue and views is going to be much higher.And then the pressure you put on yourself, like if you're living video to video,it's like you're going to feel every moment you take off just like very deeply.But if you have like a base layer where you're pulling in like enough revenueand enough views just every week on that back catalog,you've given yourself like an exhalation point to not worry about.Giving yourself reruns effectively, right? Yeah.Yeah.And then ultimately to you, those videos, even if they perform in the interim,like lower than your topical videos or your kind of like trendingvideos there, maybe there's a deepness of connectionin them too that can come across.And so not every view is, is the same in the sense of like, hey,this viewer is actually deeply connecting with meand like willing to watch a lot more videos versus yeah, I got ten timesas many viewers on this channel or on this video, but howmany of those are actually connecting with me?And like here for my point of view versus the product, right?Or the, the update.TVs have been doing season premieres for years.Like there's new movie franchises being launched.There's like debut out.Like there's like the new album is out.There's a pattern of how you launch something.I think if you don't think about it,you could be setting yourself up for disappointment. I'm notsaying you have to because like, you know, your audience, butthere's all these, like there's big gaming creatorswho take six months off every year and come back on like top of the charts.Even me, like every time I've taken a break, I think like I took three months,six months, nine months.My video, my comeback video has been like my best performing video.But you can treat it like this is going to be a premiere.Like I'm going to like talk about it before I launch it.I'm going to get people ready for it.I might like post a short, I might post like a community post,I might like talk on social about it, but get that audience excited to see you again.Yeah, I think it's a matter of scheduling, right?Because there's an interesting thing that I see happen where people view itas the break and the break ends, and I'm back at work the next day,and it's not like you shouldn't be up like break endsand I'm uploading a video.It's like build into the break, the kind of like upswing,like the coming back into it.Take some time to shoot 1 or 2 videos, plan out a live stream,whatever kind of content you post, plan for that, plan for some pop and circumstance,or plan for it to just be like the best video that itcan be when you come back.Because I think what you don't want to do is come off of an amazing breakand then thrust yourself into a South Park type like seven days to air kindor six days to air situation where you're like trying to scrambleno build in the time to also create that extra video.And you can like have your teamor be thinking about that video if you want a full disconnect, full disconnect.But like, you can also be putting all these pieces in place during your breakas kind of a more light touch situation.So that, yeah, when you come back, it feels more monumental, momentous.It feels like you are like actually reinstalling reinstitutinglike a healthier work life balance.Yeah. And I think that's a big thing too, is like,don't throw yourself back into a situation.Like if you need a break because your workload is not sustainable,don't throw yourself back into that. So coming back is as much about communicatingwith your audience and figuring out what content as coming backto something that makes sense,because otherwise it's just going to be this steady stream of kindof like sprints and then rest and sprint and rest.Yeah, I would say like,don't also think that you have to like post three videos to warmyour audience back up again and then go for the banger. Yeah.Like if you have a banger,put out the banger that is your season premiere.That's what's going to get everyone reengaged and like rewatching your videos.I mean, how many examples are there of channels that go monthswithout posting? And then when they post again and I've seen themdo it without any, it's kind of without a premier.They just post a video and it's like they've been working on this videoor they've taken some time and worked on the video and they've droppedit and people go right back to it and love it.Yeah. I mean, a lot of the big science engineering, like educational channels,it just takes them months to do the experiment or the process.And so they can only post once a month or once a quarter even.And the audience is like tens of millions of views for them every time they post.Yeah. I mean, I'm aging myself, but I think, you know, likehistory of Japan into history of the world, I guess like that'sa huge gap between videos.But it was amazing when it came backand everybody that's a very kind of obscure meme video that I came acrossfor the first time, was not familiar with the creator.And then to see that drop and then have another version come inand have it served to me, one showcases, I think,the power that the search and discovery systems will surface the videosto your audience when you come back.And two, that if your content is great,people will wait around for it because they want to see you postmore of it, and they want to be entertained by it and engage with it.Yeah, yeah. So if you break down like the algorithm is automated, word of mouth,give it something to talk about.Yeah, yeah. And I'll say shout out Bill Wurtz.Just name your content and not name you.

title: Unlocking the Business of Brand Deals on YouTube /w @HopeScope
description:
Creator @hopescope and YouTube senior director, Romana, sit down with Creator Liaison @ReneRitchie for an in-depth chat on the reality of running a YouTube channel as a business. They break down how automated midrolls actually work, the nuts and bolts of brand deals and dynamic brand segments, and what it really takes to turn a YouTube audience into a sustainable career

0:00 - The YouTube flywheel
0:36 - Hopescope’s journey to 8 million subscribers
1:24 - How YouTube ad products work: matching creators and brands
4:11 - Optimizing midrolls and overcoming creator hesitation
9:34 - The spectrum of opportunities: from takeovers to always-on partnerships
11:15 - Finding intuitive brand deals and unlocking new verticals
13:43 - Brand mentions, open calls, and getting paid
15:53 - Dynamic brand segments: monetizing long-form archives
19:42 - What's next: affiliate boosts, shorts links, and full-funnel growth
21:54 - Diversifying your business: AdSense, merch, and brand deals
23:28 - The future of hyperpersonalization and creator-brand partnerships
transcript: Hope scope has an incredible following on YouTube,going from fitness to everything that is fashion hauls and just.I'm going to say Joy on YouTube with an incredible connection to her audience.And Romana works on the ad productsand the brand products that help us as creators turn our channelsinto full fledged businesses, dare I say, empires for some of us.All of us. One day. And I'm Rene Ritchie, your creator liaison,and we're going to talk about just the power that is the YouTube flywheel of viewers,creators, and advertisers making all of our lives so much better.Hope. What is your channel about on YouTube?So my channel actually started ten years ago this summer, which is so crazy.This is a full blown career at this point.So it started out I actually reviewed activewear because fitness was huge.Fashion was huge, but nobody was really in that niche.So I was like, let's try this.And I grew my channel to about 300,000 viewers just within that littleactivewear niche. But then it got to the point where a lot of women were commentingand they were saying, oh, I like to watch you,even though I don't care about activewear.And I was like, oh, maybe I could talk about other things. So itstarted to branch off into like pop culture and fashion and beauty.And so that's kind of how Hopes Go became what it is today.And I have over 8 million subscribers, which is.Literally a haul of videos.Yeah, yeah, yeah. What do you do at YouTube?I work on product management and I'm responsible for creative partnerships,connected TV monetization as well as brand advertising.I love that. So I think like sometimes creators, we just turn ads on,maybe we turn minerals on, but we don't really think about it.And it's this whole, I just imagine like,there's a whole bunch of advertisers out there who care as muchabout their content as we care about our content.Do you see creators like having these conversations yet?Yeah, I would say now I like nerd out about ads and monetization and all that stuff,but probably for 80 or 90% of my career very much was just, oh,like, it's making money.I just kind of thought CPMs were like a stagnant random number that you got assigned,and there wasn't anything that you could do.But through my relationships at YouTube and relationships with other creators,I have learned so much.So I'm really glad that more conversations are happening for sure.I love this because I think like in a lot of industries, there's likegenerations of people to advise you.Like if you're a new hip hop artist, someone will tell you, you know,if you have explicit lyrics, you might not get iHeartRadio play,or if you make an R-rated version of this movie, it might get less box office.But I feel like as creators, we hit that face first every time.Could you give us a little insight into how, like, ads actually work as a product?Sure. I thought that was like beautifully done,very well done. Because I think itreally is what we were talking about.Creators maybe turn ads on now in the age of television,roles are more important because maybe someone is watching a 30 minuteor a 60 minute video and there just isn't as many pre-rolls, but for or CPM, like,I don't know, like auto parts maybe have a higher CPM than tech videos,but I'm not going to change my channel just for like an auto parts CPM.What can creators really do?Like how do you think about the products for ads and what we can do to optimize?I would say there are two dimensions to this.One is just, you know, running ads on your channelsand instead of figuring out where to place the ads,leave that to the technology that we have.We've enabled this with Gemini.It finds the right placement for an ad in your contentand then showing that ad to the right user in the content.So we have something that is called smart minerals and creator can opt in to that.I think that's step number one actually helps you make more money,as I'm sure you've seen as well.Hope. So. title: New! Amazon Tags in YouTube Shopping, Views (Co-Viewed), Branded Content Updates
description:
This week on YouTube creators in the US are getting the ability to add Amazon Tags to YouTube Shopping, there's a no Views (Co-Viewed) stat to better project the true scope of audiences watching on TV, and updates to the features, policies, and auto-labeling for branded content deals

2:02 - Views (Co-Viewed)

transcript: Oh, yeah. Amazon has officially joined the YouTube Shopping Affiliate Programin the US. Hello Insiders. I'm Manny Ricci an OG creator and now working atYouTube and here's what's up. To tag Amazon products and earn commission, youhave to meet the following requirements. First, be enrolled in the YouTubePartner Program. Next, be enrolled in the YouTube Shopping Affiliate Programin the United States and be part of the Amazon Influencer Program AIP or AmazonAssociate Program AAP with your account active and in good standing. Then, linkyour YouTube channel to your AIP or APP account and once that's all done, you'llbe able to tag products directly inside your videos, shorts, and live streamsand viewers can discover and shop your recommendations in a sleek,non-disruptive way while they watch. Now, here are some important detailscreators also need to know. There's a curated product catalog. Amazon providesYouTube with a curated catalog of highly requested and trending products. If youcan't find a specific product you want to tag, you can request to add it byreaching out to YouTube support. There's also auto tagging support. If you haveauto tagging enabled or choose to turn it on, YouTube systems may automaticallyreview your recent uploads to identify and tag eligible Amazon products. Andthere's aggregated analytics. You won't see breakdowns for specific products orindividual videos in your analytics, but you will see your overall daily earningsin YouTube Studio. Then, there are finalized payments. Your Amazon earningswill lock on a monthly cycle and be paid out via AdSense combined with yourstandard YouTube affiliate payments. So, for example, earnings that lock inJanuary are paid out in March. Also, there are returns and negative balances.Just like with other retailers, if a viewer returns a product, thatcommission is deducted from your balance. This can sometimes cause atemporary negative balance in your reports, which will roll over until yournext positive earning cycle. And as a reminder, when using product tags,please make sure to clearly disclose your affiliate or sponsored links inline with local advertising standards like FTC guidelines and check out theYouTube Help Center for more. That's right. We've got another new privatemetric coming to YouTube Analytics. It's called views co-viewed and it's designedto give creators a complete picture of how our content is being watchedtogether on the big TV screen. Viewers watch an average of over 1 billion hoursof YouTube on TV screens every day and they're often watching in groups withfriends and family. Until now, every TV device playback was viewed as a singleview, but views co-viewed estimates the total number of people watching on TVs.For example, a family of three watching together is reflected as three estimatedco-viewed views. And just like creators can look at views and unique views toget a better sense of not just how often a video is being seen, but how manydistinct people are seeing it, creators will be able to look at views co-viewedand unique reach introduced earlier this year to get the same insight on how ourcontent is being watched on TV. Also, views co-viewed are a platform-backedmetric, which means they can be used when negotiating brand deals torepresent the full impact and value of a creator's content on TV. Now, a fewthings you're going to want to keep in mind. Public view counts are notchanging. Views co-viewed is a private metric for creators inside YouTubeAnalytics that we can use for reporting or pitching when and how we want. Publicview counts on the watch page remain unchanged. Views co-viewed will alsohave no impact on monetization, revenue sharing and AdSense payouts, and YouTubePartner Program eligibility will continue to be based on engaged viewsand qualified views and their modeled estimates. Views co-viewed usestatistical modeling based on demographic patterns, video genre, andviewing times to predict when people are watching together. And just to beabsolutely sure that it's clear, views co-viewed compared to unique reach,while both measure TV group viewing, views co-viewed counts total watchoccasions per person. Like a family of three watching twice is six co-views,where unique reach counts individual people only once regardless of replay.So, the same family of three would be three unique reach viewers. It's reallyway simpler than it sounds. Just watch that part back as needed. Now, viewsco-viewed do require up to 48 hours to process. Because of this two-day delay,any data range that includes the last 48 hours, such as last 28 days or thismonth, will always make your views co-viewed appear lower. So, for accuratecomparisons, select a custom date range that excludes the last two days. Forexample, choose August 1 to 17 rather than rolling views. Starting August 31,2026, you'll be able to see views co-viewed alongside unique reach in theadvanced mode of YouTube Analytics. YouTube Studio is streamlining howcreators handle brand deals to keep channels fully compliant. That includespaid product placement moving to the industry standard term branded content,as well as highly requested creator controls, viewer labels, and autolabeling of branded content on new videos starting in a few months. First,precise age and geographic gating. Navigating global advertisingregulations can just be a lot. It's tough to restrict content to specificages or regions, which sometimes means having to turn down certain kinds ofbrand deals. So, YouTube is introducing granular age and geographic restrictioncontrols directly in the details page in YouTube Studio. Now, when creatorsselect yes under the paid promotion and brand section in YouTube Studio ondesktop, it'll unlock two powerful manual controls. With these controls,creators can easily address brand and regional compliance requirements.Creators can now set an optional default minimum viewer age globally, on acountry-by-country level, or restrict viewing altogether in select regions byblocking all ages. Also, there are refreshed viewer labels and policies.YouTube wants to make sure viewers have a streamlined experience whilemaintaining total transparency. So, YouTube is launching a refreshedviewer-facing disclosure label that replaces the legacy paid promotion tagwith a much cleaner look. YouTube is also revised the Help Center guidelinesto make them easier to navigate, and there will also be automated detection,and here's what to do if you as a creator disagree. So, while it remainsthe creator's responsibility to disclose paid partnerships, in the coming months,YouTube will be deploying automated systems to help maintain viewertransparency. If YouTube systems detect undeclared promotional material in avideo, it will automatically apply the new branded content viewer label onthose new videos. But, if YouTube's automated system gets it wrong and youas a creator disagree with the labeling decision, in many cases, you'll be ableto go into YouTube Studio and toggle the setting back to no. These new settingswill be available on YouTube Studio on desktop, so check them out. Let me knowyour thoughts and questions in the comments, and keep it real.

title: New! Updates to Public View Counts & Engaged Views Explained
description:
This week on YouTube we dive into updates on how public views are counted on YouTube, what that change means for viewers and brands, and what "engaged" views mean for creators, analytics, and the algorithm


0:00 - Exposure-Based Views Moving to All Formats
0:19 - August 24 Rollout & Why YouTube Is Standardizing Views
0:43 - Sponsor & Brand Deal Benefits
0:57 - How Existing & Historical Videos Are Handled
1:14 - Engaged Views in YouTube Studio & Historical Comparisons
1:32 - YPP Eligibility & Monetization Revenue Calculations
1:44 - Are Views Now the Same as Impressions?
1:58 - Autoplay on Home & Watch Pages (Views vs. Engaged Views)
2:14 - Shorts Feed: Playback vs. Engaged Views
2:26 - Addressing the "30-Second Rule" Myth
2:42 - Are Clicks the Same as Views? (Clickbait Concerns)
2:58 - Impact on CTR, AVD, Retention & Recommendations
transcript: YouTube is moving to an exposure-based model for views across all formats.Meaning, a view will now be counted the moment a video begins to play from thevery first frame. Hello, insiders. I'm René Ritchie, a long-time creator nowworking at YouTube, and here's what's up. Last year, YouTube moved to anexposure-based model for Shorts views. This year, starting August 24, YouTubewill be expanding that model to long-form, podcasts, live streams, allformats. YouTube is doing this to ensure consistency across the platform, to makesure every moment of connection between creator and audience is captured, and sothat there's no confusion or fragmentation about what a view actuallymeans. Creators can use this updated, standardized count to better understandviews across formats, and to better communicate the full scale of audienceimpact to brand partners and sponsors. And viewers will know when they see aview count, it's all based on the same model, from that first frame. All newvideos uploaded after the changes on August 24, 2026, will show the updatedfirst frame view count. All videos uploaded prior to the change will keeptheir existing view count up until the change. Historical view totals will notbe updated retroactively, but following the change, new views on those videoswill follow the updated first frame count. To compare performance moreconsistently before and after the change, creators can use the engagedviews metric in YouTube Studio. An engaged view means the viewer stayed towatch past the first frame and initial seconds. It's how all views were countedhistorically, which is why they're useful for historical comparisons.Engaged views will also remain the view metric used to qualify for Shorts ad andpremium revenue sharing in the YouTube Partner Program, and for monetizationand revenue calculation across all videos. Let's break down the mostimportant questions that you might have about this change. Are views now thesame as an impression? If you see a thumbnail recommended on the home pageor suggested on the watch page, and you don't interact with it in any way, thatremains an impression, not a view. If you see a thumbnail recommended on thehomepage or suggested on the watch page and you hover over it and it starts toauto play, that is now counted as a view from the very first frame. And if youlet it keep playing for some amount of seconds after that first frame, it's anengaged view. Same for a short in the shorts feed. The moment it starts toplay, it's a view. If you let it keep playing for some amount of seconds afterthat first frame, it's an engaged view. Now, I've heard some people say itpreviously took 30 seconds for a view to be counted and that's simply not thecase. YouTube doesn't specify exactly how many seconds because it can varyacross services and YouTube also doesn't want anyone focusing on gaming themetric, just making the most satisfying experience possible for viewers. So, areclicks now the same as views? If you click on a thumbnail and you start towatch the video, that was a view before, it's a view now and it's also an engagedview. No change or difference there. So, if you're concerned at all that thisupdate would incentivize clickbait, hopefully that addresses that concern.I've also seen some people worry about how this change will affect things likeclick-through rate, average view duration or other metrics. And the TLDRis it doesn't. The vast majority of analytics remain anchored on engagedviews. So, no change to CTR, AVD, retention. Likewise, no change torecommendations, to the algorithm and no change to the YouTube Partner Program.That's based on qualified views and for more information on those, hit up therelated video link. Then, jump in the comments, let me know your thoughts andquestions and keep it real.

title: Therapist Georgia Dow's Screen Time Tips for Parents
description:
Creator, educator, and psychotherapist @GeorgiaDow chats with Creator Insideer @ReneRitchie about how parents can spark conversation over shared videos, how YouTube factors into her therapy practice, parental controls and handling boundaries, the point system she used for screen time with her own children, and the value of modeling behavior for kids

00:00 - Introduction: Preparing Kids for Media
00:10 - Georgia's Channel Mission and Background
00:18 - Sparking Family Conversations Through Shared Videos

05:42 - Modeling Behavior and Media Literacy
transcript: Our job as parents is not to protect our kids from media. It's not to protect ourkids from all of the world around them. It's to prepare them for it.>> Who are you and what is your channel about?>> I'm Jordan Dow and I'm a psychotherapist and I run a channel that analyzes all ofthe media that we consume and the psychology behind it.>> What do you hope families are getting out of your channel when they'rewatching your videos together? >> When we watch TV and consume mediatogether, we end up with these wonderful parental moments. I make videos. I likewatching videos and I also want to make sure that I'm having my children haveage-appropriate experiences. And I think that you can use watching differentvideos as a wonderful learning experience. If they feel reactive tosomething, why do they feel reactive to it? What is the purpose of this video?How do they handle complex emotions? How would they debate this subjectthemselves? And so I think that having the different conversations with yourkids about what are they watching, being able to go through how can they look atthings with a critical eye? Plus, I think it's really important for parentsto know what is the media that their children are watching and why. What Ihope that they get from it is a great conversation into what are they takingfrom these thoughts and theories. I think that sometimes as parents we wantto just give our children the answers, but it's also important to ask them thequestions and let them come up with their own answers and to figure out whythey feel that way. >> How have you, like whether it is as aparent or as an educator or as a psychotherapist, how have you integratedYouTube and video into your teaching, your parenting, your practice?>> I actually use YouTube a lot. I think that YouTube is a wonderful learningtool. I will put on a social situation and I'll say, "What would you do? How doyou feel when you're going through that?" Because my job as apsychotherapist is be able to look through other people's eyes, be able tosee the world from their viewpoint. And so, because of that, it helps me be ableto empathize better and to be able to give them better tools. Also, forchildren, you can actually take a look at what do they care about? What makesthem feel good? Sometimes, if we're going through something and it'ssomething that's very scary for them, I'll say, "You know what? Let's justwatch this silly video or laugh or be relaxed." Today on The Colin & Samir Show we sit down with Markiplier and YouTube's Tim Katz, live from the Fox Studios lot in front of 650 creators at Press Publish LA: The Hollywood Creator Summit.
After more than 15 years building one of YouTube's most personal channels, Markiplier put Hollywood on notice with Iron Lung, the horror film he financed, wrote, directed, and starred in. The film pulled in close to $52 million in theaters and is now on YouTube. We get into why he treated a feature film like a YouTube video, what he learned leading a hundred-person crew, why he stays his own harshest critic, and how he sees this collision of YouTube and Hollywood playing out for creators.

transcript: I never thought that the same channel where I was crying with joy over reaching 10 million views would, shortly after, receive a demonetization message. But my story does not begin here. My journey started with a small animated story video. I uploaded my first video. And I had absolutely no idea that this video would go so viral. Some time later, I opened the studio and in front of me were about 4.9 million views. I truly couldn't believe it, but behind a viral video, there isn't just one click. Behind it are scripts, characters, animation, editing, and a lot of hard work. But the happiness lasted only for a few days. Someone else copied my script to make their own animation, and they got 11 million views. I actually broke down in tears. To steal someone's hard work and ideas like that. My heart was broken. But I thought maybe it was just their luck. I will not quit my work. I continued to make videos. I improved the stories and kept working consistently on my channel. Then, slowly, my channel started moving towards the 10 million views milestone. It started growing. When the 10 million views appeared in the studio, that same number didn't immediately show up in the earnings section. I waited and kept waiting. Then, after waiting for about a month, the 10 million finally started appearing in the earnings section too. And that day, without delay, I applied for monetization. The first step was to accept YouTube's terms and rules. I accepted them carefully. The second step was the AdSense account. I already had an AdSense account, so I attached it to my channel, and then came the third step: Get Reviewed. This is where my real waiting began.>> I was watching videos by other creators . Many people were saying that their review was done in just two or three days. But for me, two or three days turned into 5, 10, and then almost 20 days. Still, no email arrived. I contacted YouTube Live Support. I explained my situation and asked why my review was taking so long. I was told that there could be a delay. A delay could happen due to a high volume of applications. I waited anyway. And before I knew it, this waiting period reached nearly 2 months. After such a long wait, I finally received an update from YouTube. But the email I was waiting for wasn't what I had imagined it would be. Yeah. My channel has been demonetized. And the reason given is satisfying or off-putting content. The moment I had been waiting for so long, at that very moment, all my happiness just vanished. This journey taught me that going viral and getting monetized are two different things. Just getting views does not guarantee approval. If you are also a creator, don't just run after views. Create original and valuable content. And if a decision comes from YouTube, don't panic. First, understand the reason and then follow the correct appeal process. I shared this journey so you could know that a creator's life looks easy from the outside, but it is very difficult on the inside. Started with 4.9 million views. Reached up to 10 million. Applied for monetization. Waited for about 2 months. But I am not giving up yet. I am waiting for the appeal and hope that my content will be reviewed correctly. If you are following my journey, please pray for me. Support me and share this video. Thank you for staying with me.

transcript: If you’re in the YouTube Partner Program and want to make money through ads, your content needs to follow our Advertiser-friendly Content Guidelines. Advertisers come to YouTube to connect with potential customers, and it’s important to them that their ads only show against content that aligns with their brand. That’s why we have Advertiser-friendly Content Guidelines, to help ensure that YouTube remains a safe place for brands to reach their target audiences – which in turn helps creators earn more money.Let’s walk through: how advertiser-friendly content guidelines work, how you can check your monetization status & what each status icon means, and a deep dive about the Yellow Icon status specifically.First, how advertiser-friendly content guidelines work on YouTube?When it comes to earning through ads with your channel, there are specific rules about: What can run all ads What can run limited ads And what will not run any ads, and should have monetization turned offAdvertiser-friendly content is appropriate for most audiences, and there are many sensitive topics that impact advertiser-friendliness, including things like: Inappropriate language, Violence, Adult content, and more.Each of these topics have Ads Guidance terms that indicate whether your content: can earn regular ad revenue; may earn limited or no ad revenue; or will definitely not earn any ad revenue. So it’s important to familiarize yourself with these policy details in our YouTube Help Center, and remember that these guidelines apply to all of your content on YouTube – including your videos, Shorts, live streams, titles, thumbnails, tags, and descriptions.Compliance with our Ad-friendly content guidelines is evaluated during the upload process, with a combination of automated systems and human review.It’s important to note that context is very important. If there’s educational, documentary, scientific, or artistic value, that may change a video’s suitability for advertisers. For example, artistic content like music videos may contain elements like inappropriate language, references to soft drug use, or non-explicit sexual themes, but still be suitable for advertising. Adding context helps us make the correct monetization decision. Keep in mind that videos without a title or metadata may not give enough context to help our systems understand if the content is suitable for all advertisers.When you’re monetizing, you’ll also get access to Self-Certification – which becomes part of the upload flow if you have Monetization turned on. At the “Ad-Suitability” step, Self-Certification asks you to rate your videos against our advertiser-friendly content guidelines. We then use your input to help decide the ad suitability of your videos. The goal of Self-Certification is to help reduce errors with our automatic reviews, and help your videos get monetized more accurately from the start.Next, how can you check your monetization status & what does each status icon mean?You can check your video’s monetization status by going to YouTube Studio, then “Content”. In the Monetization column, you’ll find monetization icons. You can hover over the icons for more info about what each one means. Here’s a quick breakdown:A green icon with “On” will show if monetization is on, and your content meets our advertiser-friendly content guidelines. This icon means your video is eligible for most ads. A clock icon with “Checking” will show when our systems are checking for ad suitability. While the ad suitability check is in progress, we don’t show ads on your video. So we recommend uploading your content as Private or Unlisted first, so you can wait to see what the monetization status will be before publishing. A red icon with “Ineligible” will show if monetization is off and cannot be turned on. For example, this icon will show in cases of some copyright claims. When you see this icon, your video will not earn from ads, and will not be eligible to earn from YouTube Premium subscription revenue. A gray icon with “Off” will show if monetization is turned off, but can still be turned on. This icon means you did not choose to turn monetization on. Or, if you get this icon on your Shorts, it means that you haven't accepted the Shorts Monetization Module in YouTube Studio yet. And lastly, a yellow icon with “Limited” will show if you turned monetization on, but your content will have limited or no ads. This means your content doesn’t meet all of our advertiser-friendly content guidelines. Because brands can choose to opt out of content that doesn’t meet our advertiser-friendly content guidelines, your content may earn less revenue compared to content that does meet the guidelines. When you see this icon, your video is still eligible to earn YouTube Premium subscription revenue.Now, let’s dive a bit more into the Yellow Monetization Icon.In YouTube Studio from the Content tab, you can filter by Monetization, then “Limited” to see videos that have a yellow monetization icon. In the Restrictions column, you’ll see “Ad suitability”. If you hover over that, there are a few different statuses you might see. Here’s a breakdown of what the statuses mean:If the status says “Ad suitability” with the option for “Request Review”: That means our systems assessed this video. However, our systems don’t always get it right. If our systems mark your video as not suitable for all advertisers, and you disagree, you can request another review by a policy specialist. They’ll review the decision made by our systems. If appropriate, they can change the video’s monetization status. If they complete their review and agree with the system’s decision, in YouTube Studio, the monetization status will remain. If you used Self Certification during the upload flow, you’ll see what issues our expert found that led to a yellow icon. Your appeal decision may also provide timestamps of where in the video issues appeared -- or a note indicating if the issue was with your title or thumbnail. Note that these timestamps aren’t exhaustive. The additional context given is to help you better understand where our experts found policy violations in your content. Timestamps do not offer direction on where to make edits, but help offer greater clarity on policy violations. Videos, thumbnails, and titles edited with YouTube Studio to remove violative content won't be eligible for re-review. Note that videos that aren’t rated by Self Certification in the upload flow won't be eligible to see these timestamps. If the status description says “Ad suitability - Under review”: That means you already requested another review, and a policy specialist is actively reviewing the video. The specialist can keep or change the monetization status, and their decision is final. If the status description says “Ad suitability - confirmed by review”: That means that our policy specialists finished reviewing the video, and have confirmed that it doesn’t meet our advertiser-friendly content guidelines. The yellow icon status can’t be changed.Now let’s dive into a few questions you might have when it comes to Yellow Icons and reviews.How can creators request a review? From a desktop: Go to YouTube Studio, then Content. You can search for the specific video you’re looking for. Or, you can filter by Monetization status on this page, and select “Limited” to see videos that might be eligible for review. Once you’ve found the video you want, go to the Restrictions column for that video, and hover over Ad suitability. Click REQUEST REVIEW, and follow the on-screen instructions. From a mobile device: Go to the YouTube Studio app, then Content. You can search for the specific video you’re looking for. Or, you can filter by Monetization status on this page, and select “Limited” to see videos that might be eligible for review. Once you’ve found the video you want, tap into it. Tap on the section that shows the monetization status. The tap “Request review”, and follow the on-screen instructions How does the review process work? When you request a review, an expert looks at the video. They spend time watching the video and review its content, title, and metadata against our advertiser-friendly content guidelines. Our reviewers evaluate the video and related content as a whole. During their review, specialists use the advertiser-friendly guidelines paired with the following principles: Context Focus Tone Realism And Graphicness The most important principle is context. What’s the intention behind your video — is it to inform and educate, or to shock and incite? For example, if it’s to inform and educate, then you should include context in your title, thumbnails, description, and tags. This context helps reviewers make the right monetization decision. Without context, reviewers may not accurately assess your content. Once the review is complete, you’ll get an email with the monetization decision. How long do reviews take? We know that these reviews are important to you and your revenue. Additional reviews typically take up to 7 days. Be sure to check your email, as this is how we send the monetization decision once the review is complete.We hope this helps you learn more about our Advertiser-friendly Content Guidelines, how they’re applied, and the systems put in place to help you make informed decisions. To learn more, check out the links in the description. Thanks for watching.
